expectedText:
TRADEMARK LICENSE AGREEMENT
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · Beta Distributors, LLC

GRANT OF LICENSE
Acme, Inc. ("Licensor") owns the trademark described as follows: The word mark "ACME" and associated logo, U.S. Reg. No. 1,234,567 (the "Mark"). Licensor grants to Beta Distributors, LLC ("Licensee") a license to use the Mark solely in connection with the goods and/or services, and within the geographic territory, described in this agreement. This license is personal to Licensee and may not be assigned, sublicensed, or transferred without Licensor's prior written consent. All use of the Mark by Licensee, and all goodwill arising from that use, shall inure to the benefit of Licensor.

WHAT COUNTS AS A "TRADEMARK" UNDER FEDERAL LAW
Federal trademark law (the Lanham Act) defines a “trademark” broadly, as any word, name, symbol, or device — or combination of these — used by a person, or that a person has a bona fide intention to use, to identify and distinguish that person's goods from goods made or sold by others and to indicate the source of the goods, even if the source is unknown to the public. This statutory definition is what makes The word mark "ACME" and associated logo, U.S. Reg. No. 1,234,567 the kind of thing federal trademark law protects and regulates, and it is the backdrop against which a license — permission from Acme, Inc., as the mark's owner, for Beta Distributors, LLC to use it — operates.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The term “trademark” includes any word, name, symbol, or device, or any combination thereof— (1) used by a person, or (2) which a person has a bona fide intention to use in commerce and applies to register on the principal register established by this chapter, to identify and distinguish his or her goods, including a unique product, from those manufactured or sold by others and to indicate the source of the goods, even if that source is unknown."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1127 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Lanham Act definitions — "trademark" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1127)
  Known gap: This is federal law (the Lanham Act, which applies nationwide, not just in California), used as real evidence of the statutory definition of "trademark" — not a claim that the mark described in this agreement has been examined here for whether it actually qualifies for trademark protection or registration, which depends on facts such as distinctiveness and actual use in commerce that this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1127); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHY A LICENSEE'S USE CAN BENEFIT THE LICENSOR — ONLY WITH QUALITY CONTROL
Under federal trademark law, a licensee's use of a mark can legally count as the trademark owner's own use — meaning it can support and benefit the owner's trademark rights, rather than creating a separate, competing claim to the mark — but only where that use is by a “related company,” a term the statute defines as a person whose use of the mark is controlled by the owner with respect to the nature and quality of the goods or services the mark is used on. A separate statutory provision confirms that where a mark is used by such related companies, that use inures to the benefit of the registrant, provided the mark is not used in a way that deceives the public. This is the statutory basis for allowing Beta Distributors, LLC's use of The word mark "ACME" and associated logo, U.S. Reg. No. 1,234,567 to support, rather than undermine, Acme, Inc.'s trademark rights — and it is expressly conditioned on Acme, Inc. actually controlling the nature and quality of what Beta Distributors, LLC sells or offers under the mark.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The term “related company” means any person whose use of a mark is controlled by the owner of the mark with respect to the nature and quality of the goods or services on or in connection with which the mark is used."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1127 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Lanham Act definitions — "related company" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1127)
  "Where a registered mark or a mark sought to be registered is or may be used legitimately by related companies, such use shall inure to the benefit of the registrant or applicant for registration, and such use shall not affect the validity of such mark or of its registration, provided such mark is not used in such manner as to deceive the public."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1055 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, use by related companies (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1055)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory “related company” and inurement mechanism — not a claim that any particular licensing arrangement in fact involves the level of control the statute requires, which is a fact question this clause does not resolve. This clause cites two provisions of the same Lanham Act definitional/inurement scheme (15 U.S.C. § 1127's definition of "related company" and 15 U.S.C. § 1055's inurement rule); they are cited together because § 1055 uses the term § 1127 defines, and no independent second source exists for a two-provision statutory mechanism like this one. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

QUALITY CONTROL
Licensee agrees that all goods and/or services offered under the Mark will meet quality standards materially consistent with those Licensor has established for goods and/or services bearing the Mark. Licensor, or its designated representative, may request samples of Licensee's goods or services bearing the Mark and may inspect Licensee's use of the Mark on reasonable notice, to confirm this standard is being met. If Licensor reasonably determines that Licensee's use of the Mark fails to meet this standard, Licensor may notify Licensee in writing, and Licensee shall correct the deficiency within the time period stated in that notice. Nothing in this agreement transfers ownership of the Mark to Licensee, and Licensee's use of the Mark, and any goodwill it generates, exists solely for Licensor's benefit and reverts fully to Licensor upon termination of this agreement.

"NAKED LICENSING" AND THE RISK OF LOSING THE MARK
Courts have held that a trademark owner who licenses a mark without exercising adequate quality control over the licensee's use of it risks losing rights in the mark altogether, through a doctrine commonly called “naked licensing.” The Ninth Circuit has explained that a trademark owner may grant a license and remain protected only if quality control over the goods or services sold under the mark by the licensee is maintained; uncontrolled, or “naked,” licensing can result in the mark ceasing to function as a symbol of consistent quality and a controlled source, and where a licensor fails to exercise adequate quality control, a court may find that the owner has abandoned the mark — an involuntary forfeiture that does not require any intent by the owner to give up the mark. In the case the Ninth Circuit was deciding, the trademark owner's licensing agreements contained no quality-control provisions, and the owner's evidence of any actual control over the licensee's product — occasional informal tastings and reliance on a now-deceased winemaker's reputation — was held insufficient, resulting in cancellation of the registration for abandonment. This is why Acme, Inc. exercising, and being able to show it exercised, real quality control over Beta Distributors, LLC's use of The word mark "ACME" and associated logo, U.S. Reg. No. 1,234,567 is treated by courts as more than a formality.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“[a] trademark owner may grant a license and remain protected provided quality control of the goods and services sold under the trademark by the licensee is maintained.” ... But “[u]ncontrolled or ‘naked’ licensing may result in the trademark ceasing to function as a symbol of quality and controlled source.” ... Consequently, where the licensor fails to exercise adequate quality control over the licensee, “a court may find that the trademark owner has abandoned the trademark, in which case the owner would be estopped from asserting rights to the trademark.”"
  — Barcamerica International USA Trust v. Tyfield Importers, Inc., 289 F.3d 589 (9th Cir. 2002) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/7105028/barcamerica-international-usa-trust-v-tyfield-importers-inc/)
  "A mark shall be deemed to be “abandoned” if either of the following occurs: ... (2) When any course of conduct of the owner, including acts of omission as well as commission, causes the mark to become the generic name for the goods or services on or in connection with which it is used or otherwise to lose its significance as a mark."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1127 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of "abandoned" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1127)
  Known gap: "Naked licensing" is not itself a phrase used in the Lanham Act; it is a judicial doctrine that courts have built on the Act's statutory definition of "abandoned" (15 U.S.C. § 1127), which includes when a mark owner's course of conduct causes a mark to lose its significance as a mark, and on 15 U.S.C. § 1064(3), which allows a registration to be cancelled at any time on abandonment grounds. This clause cites Ninth Circuit precedent (Barcamerica), which is binding only within that circuit; other circuits apply the same general naked-licensing doctrine but the exact standard for how much control is "adequate" can vary and is decided case by case on the specific facts of the licensing relationship, none of which this clause resolves for any particular license.

ABANDONMENT AS A GROUND FOR CANCELLING A REGISTERED MARK
Federal trademark law allows a petition to cancel a registered mark to be filed at any time — with no time limit — if the registered mark has been abandoned, among other grounds such as the mark becoming generic or its registration having been obtained fraudulently. Because abandonment includes the naked-licensing scenario courts have recognized, an uncontrolled license of The word mark "ACME" and associated logo, U.S. Reg. No. 1,234,567 is not merely a private contract problem between Acme, Inc. and Beta Distributors, LLC; it can expose the underlying registration itself to a cancellation proceeding brought by a third party, at any time, regardless of how long the registration has otherwise stood unchallenged.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A petition to cancel a registration of a mark ... may ... be filed as follows by any person who believes that he is or will be damaged ... by the registration of a mark on the principal register ...: ... (3) At any time if the registered mark becomes the generic name for the goods or services, or a portion thereof, for which it is registered, or is functional, or has been abandoned, or its registration was obtained fraudulently ..."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1064(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, grounds for cancellation of a registered mark (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1064)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that abandonment (of which naked licensing is one judicially recognized species, per the clause above) is a codified cancellation ground with no time limit — not a claim that any particular license under this agreement will in fact be challenged, or that a cancellation petition would succeed, which depends on facts about actual quality control this clause does not resolve. The task brief that prompted this research guessed this ground might appear at 15 U.S.C. § 1064(5); on checking the statutory text directly, the "at any time" abandonment ground is actually in § 1064(3), not § 1064(5) — this clause cites the section as verified, not as assumed. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1064(3)); no additional independent source was found for this.

TRADEMARK LICENSES HAVE NO STATUTORY WRITING REQUIREMENT
Unlike a copyright transfer, which federal copyright law requires to be in a signed writing to be valid, the Lanham Act contains no comparable statutory provision requiring a trademark license to be in writing. The Lanham Act does require an assignment of a registered mark — an outright transfer of ownership — to be by a written instrument, but that writing requirement applies to assignments of ownership, not to licenses, which merely grant permission to use a mark the owner continues to own. Putting a license like this one for The word mark "ACME" and associated logo, U.S. Reg. No. 1,234,567 in writing is common practice, and is generally the only practical way to establish and prove the quality-control terms the naked-licensing doctrine looks for, but doing so is a matter of prudence and contract practice, not a freestanding federal statutory mandate the way it is for a copyright transfer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Assignments shall be by instruments in writing duly executed."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, assignment of marks — writing requirement (contrast with licenses) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1060)
  Known gap: This clause reports an absence — the lack of a statutory writing requirement for trademark licenses specifically — confirmed by reviewing the relevant Lanham Act provisions (15 U.S.C. §§ 1055, 1060, 1127) directly rather than assuming it; it does not cite a provision imposing a writing requirement because none was found for licenses. This is federal law that applies nationwide; it does not address whether any state's general contract-law statute of frauds might separately require a writing for an agreement like this one depending on its terms or duration, which is a separate body of law this clause does not cover.
